title: Castling

D0.outcome: Describes castling: the king moves two squares towards a rook and the rook jumps to the other side of it, only if neither piece has moved.

D1.outcome: When told 'castle', castles on the right side, kingside or queenside, for both colours.

D2.outcome: Decides whether castling is legal right now and says why not (right lost, piece in between, king in check, or a square the king crosses or lands on is attacked), knowing that an attacked rook or an attacked b-square does not stop it.

D3.outcome: Says whether castling will still be possible after a few given moves, noticing which moves lose the right for good.

misconceptions: You may castle out of check.
You cannot castle if the rook is attacked.
A king or rook that has moved and come back may still castle.
Castling is allowed whenever the squares between are empty.
conditions: Castling needs: neither king nor that rook has moved, the squares between them empty, the king not in check, and the squares the king crosses and lands on not attacked.
Only the squares the king uses matter for attacks; the rook, and on the queen side the square beside the rook, may be attacked.
contrasts: The king may not pass over an attacked square, even if it would land on a safe one.
An attacked rook, or an attacked b-square, does not stop queenside castling.
